rationale: A wins because it keeps the story honest while still finding real conflict, data, governance, and pricing angles. Its best line, "The auto-renewal has an adversary now: Ramp's agent drafts the cancellation email," is sharp and grounded in the product mechanics. B keeps stepping over the facts: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" turns a human-approved draft into autonomous action, which is exactly the kind of exaggeration that gets a founder embarrassed on reply one.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp gives away software-spend auditing for free, and plans to charge enterprises later" slightly overstates the update. The facts say an enterprise tier is coming later this year, not that Ramp has announced paid pricing.

"The AI agent's biggest savings didn't come from negotiating. They came from cancelling." Good angle, but the update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals; it does not prove realized cancellations beat renegotiations yet.
"the 200-company beta is the first public dataset behind it" is plausible launch logic, but not explicitly supplied. Small overreach, still an overreach.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp's new AI agent emails vendors" is wrong on the key mechanic. The update says the agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves; it does not send them itself.
"The average company wastes $342,000 a year" generalizes from Ramp's 200-company beta to the market. That is how internal data becomes fake market data in a blazer.
"software it forgot to cancel" flattens the stated sources of savings. The update says unused seats and auto-renewals, plus duplicate seats; forgetting to cancel is only one slice.

"Spend visibility alone didn't save these 200 companies" rests on a made-up premise. B admits it needs confirmation that beta companies were existing Ramp customers with prior spend visibility, which means the headline should not exist yet.
